Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats hallucination as generated content that is factually incorrect, fabricated, nonsensical, misleading, or unfaithful, especially when it is not grounded in the input, source context, retrieved evidence, training facts, or established world knowledge. Many papers count it whenever an output adds unsupported material, contradicts the source or ground truth, fails to convey the queried fact, or contains any ungrounded span. A smaller line of work narrows the criterion to setting-specific failures, such as answering false-premise or unanswerable questions instead of recognizing unanswerability, inventing tools or parameters, fabricating numbers or equations, producing hallucinated observations, citing non-existent legal sections, or declaring a task complete when required steps remain undone.

Variants. A recurring set of variants appears in multimodal work, especially object, action, visual, and cross-modal hallucination, where models mention absent objects, events, sounds, attributes, positions, or other scene details. Another recurring family appears in reasoning and agent settings, including hallucinated reasoning paths and explanations, hallucinated tool calling, soliloquizing, and hallucinatory success. Papers also study source-conditioned forms in summarization, simplification, question answering, code, and literature review, using names such as factual inconsistency, confusion, in-document and out-document hallucinations, false preambles, hallucinated citations or references, and knowledge hallucination.

Space of elicitation and scores. Hallucination is measured by 29 linked instruments. The most frequently linked are POPE, CHAIR, MMHal-Bench, TruthfulQA, and AMBER: papers use these to test object existence or caption errors, response-level hallucination across question types, truthful factual question answering, and existence, attribute, or relation hallucinations. Other papers also use judge-based scoring with GPT-4 or other LLMs, manual annotation, and additional benchmark or detection suites.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers link hallucination to 46 constructs, most often Factuality and Faithfulness, and then Reliability, Trustworthiness, and Multimodal alignment. The dominant pattern ties hallucination to low factuality or low faithfulness: papers describe it as related to these constructs, some use factuality-oriented evaluations to measure it, and some claim causal relationships between Hallucination and Factuality or Faithfulness. A second recurring pattern links Hallucination to Reliability and Trustworthiness, usually through related links or papers claiming a causal relationship from Hallucination to those constructs, while multimodal papers connect it to Multimodal alignment by claiming that misalignment can lead to Hallucination; overall, papers do not converge on a single construct it reflects.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the prevailing usage treats hallucination as generated content that is factually incorrect, fabricated, nonsensical, misleading, or unfaithful, especially when it is not grounded in the input, source context, retrieved evidence, training facts, or established world knowledge. Many papers count it whenever an output adds unsupported material, contradicts the source or ground truth, fails to convey the queried fact, or contains any ungrounded span. A smaller line of work narrows the criterion to setting-specific failures, such as answering false-premise or unanswerable questions instead of recognizing unanswerability, inventing tools or parameters, fabricating numbers or equations, producing hallucinated observations, citing non-existent legal sections, or declaring a task complete when required steps remain undone.

characterization_sections.label: Variants.
characterization_sections.text: A recurring set of variants appears in multimodal work, especially object, action, visual, and cross-modal hallucination, where models mention absent objects, events, sounds, attributes, positions, or other scene details. Another recurring family appears in reasoning and agent settings, including hallucinated reasoning paths and explanations, hallucinated tool calling, soliloquizing, and hallucinatory success. Papers also study source-conditioned forms in summarization, simplification, question answering, code, and literature review, using names such as factual inconsistency, confusion, in-document and out-document hallucinations, false preambles, hallucinated citations or references, and knowledge hallucination.

characterization_sections.label: Space of elicitation and scores.
characterization_sections.text: Hallucination is measured by 29 linked instruments. The most frequently linked are POPE, CHAIR, MMHal-Bench, TruthfulQA, and AMBER: papers use these to test object existence or caption errors, response-level hallucination across question types, truthful factual question answering, and existence, attribute, or relation hallucinations. Other papers also use judge-based scoring with GPT-4 or other LLMs, manual annotation, and additional benchmark or detection suites.

characterization_sections.label: What it is taken as evidence of.
characterization_sections.text: Papers link hallucination to 46 constructs, most often Factuality and Faithfulness, and then Reliability, Trustworthiness, and Multimodal alignment. The dominant pattern ties hallucination to low factuality or low faithfulness: papers describe it as related to these constructs, some use factuality-oriented evaluations to measure it, and some claim causal relationships between Hallucination and Factuality or Faithfulness. A second recurring pattern links Hallucination to Reliability and Trustworthiness, usually through related links or papers claiming a causal relationship from Hallucination to those constructs, while multimodal papers connect it to Multimodal alignment by claiming that misalignment can lead to Hallucination; overall, papers do not converge on a single construct it reflects.
